title: Why does wind blow in a circle around a storm?
teaches: Why doesn’t the air rush straight into a low and fill it? Air sliding from high pressure to low, the spinning Earth turning under it, the balance that sends the wind along the isobars, and the fast river of wind overhead that steers storms.

blocks.title: The big ideas of this lesson
points: Air is pushed from high pressure towards low, straight across the **isobars**, and hardest where they crowd together.

The Earth turns under moving air, so over long distances the air drifts to the **right** of its path in the northern half of the world, and to the left in the southern half. The turn is strongest at the poles and vanishes at the equator.
The push and the turn balance when the wind blows **along** the isobars, with the low on its left. That is why a storm’s winds circle it instead of filling it.

Near the ground, **friction** slows the wind and the push wins a little: the wind leaks in across the isobars, the air piles up in the low and rises, and rises into cloud. Around a high, air sinks and spreads out: clear skies.
High up, the wind is fastest where cold polar air meets warm tropical air: the **jet stream**. It steers storms east, and moves south in winter and north in summer.

blocks.text: Lesson 6 gave a sailor’s rule: stand with your back to the wind, and the low is on your left. It works almost everywhere north of the equator, but it is a strange rule. If a low is a hollow in the air, why doesn’t the wind blow straight into it and fill it up, the way water runs into a hole in the sand? This lesson answers that, and it needs only two ideas: air slides from high pressure to low, and the ground underneath it turns.

Pressure, from Lesson 6, is the weight of the air overhead. Where more air is piled above a place, the pressure there is higher. Air is a fluid, and a fluid squeezed by the weight above it pushes in every direction, sideways as much as down, as you feel in your ears at the bottom of a swimming pool. So air under a deep pile pushes outward, towards places where the pile is shallower, much as water in a tank sloshes from the deep end towards the shallow one. The difference in pressure between two places is a push on the air between them.

A weather map draws pressure as **isobars**: lines joining places where the barometer reads the same, usually every 4 hPa (hectopascals, the unit of Lesson 6’s barometer: about 1,013 at sea level on an ordinary day). They work like the contour lines on a hiking map. A low is a hollow, a high is a hill, and the push on the air runs straight downhill, across the lines. Where the lines crowd together, the slope is steep and the push is strong: lines twice as close make twice the push. Where they spread out, it is gentle.[^gradient]

blocks.caption: Isobars round a low (L) and a high (H). The orange arrows show the push on the air: across the lines, from high to low.

blocks.text: If the push were all there was, the air would run straight downhill into the low, faster and faster. A low a thousand kilometres across would fill up and be gone within a day. Real lows last for days, and on any weather map the wind arrows run nearly *along* the isobars, not across them. Something turns the wind.

Picture two children on a spinning playground roundabout, facing each other across it. One rolls a ball straight at the other. To someone watching from a bench, the ball rolls in a perfectly straight line. But while it rolls, the roundabout turns, and by the time the ball reaches the far side, the friend has moved on. To the children riding along, the ball curved away, though nothing pushed it sideways.

blocks.caption: A ball rolled straight across a spinning turntable, seen from the ceiling and from on board. The violet stripe is painted on the disc.
blocks.task: Give the turntable some spin, then ride along and watch the ball swerve. Try spinning it the other way, as the Southern Hemisphere does.

blocks.text: The Earth is a turntable too. Seen from above the North Pole, it turns anticlockwise once a day, and everything standing on it turns with it. Air that moves freely over long distances is like the ball: it keeps going in a straight line, while the ground underneath turns. To us, riding the ground, the air seems to drift to the **right** of where it was heading, in the northern half of the world. South of the equator, where the Earth seen from below the South Pole turns the other way, it drifts to the left. Lesson 6 gave this its name, the **Coriolis effect**: the turning ground makes anything moving freely over it seem to swerve, always sideways, at right angles to the way it is going.

How much the ground turns under you depends on where you stand. Imagine lying on your back on the ground, looking straight up, and ask how fast the world spins around you like a record under a needle. At the North Pole, it spins a full circle every day: you are at the middle of the turntable. At the equator, you are carried round the Earth’s axis at great speed, but you are on the rim of the wheel, rolling over end to end: the ground does not spin around you at all, so there is no drift. In between it spins part of a circle a day. At 47° north, in eastern Washington, it is about three quarters of a circle (the sine of the latitude, for those who like trigonometry).

blocks.caption: How much the ground turns about your feet in a day, by latitude.

blocks.text: The drift is tiny. The Earth turns once a day, so over the few seconds that water takes to leave a sink, it turns a fraction of a degree: the sink’s shape and the way it was filled decide which way the water swirls, not the Earth.[^sinks] The turn only adds up for things that travel hundreds of kilometres over hours: winds, ocean currents, and the paths of storms. For those, it rules everything.

parts.title: Round the low, not into it

blocks.text: Now put the two ideas together. Air near a low starts to slide downhill, towards the low. As soon as it moves, the turning Earth bends it to its right. The faster it goes, the harder the turn bends it. Where does it end up? Try it below before reading on.

blocks.caption: Air starting from rest on a map of isobars, low to the north. The orange line is its path over a few hours.
blocks.task: Guess first. Then turn the Earth’s spin all the way up, and add friction with the ground.

blocks.text: It keeps bending until it runs along the isobars, with the low on its left. There the push towards the low and the turn away from it are equal and opposite, and the wind blows on along the lines without filling the low in.

This balance, wind running along the isobars because the push and the turn cancel, is called the **geostrophic wind**[^geostrophic]. It is why the wind in the northern half of the world goes anticlockwise round a low. It is also the reason for Lesson 6’s rule: if the wind runs along the isobars with the low on its left, then with your back to the wind, the low is on your left.

Near the ground, there is a third player: **friction**. Trees, hills, buildings and waves drag on the wind and slow it down. A slower wind is turned less, so the push towards the low wins a little, and the wind slants across the isobars into the low: by 10° to 20° over the sea, and by 25° to 40° over rough land. The drag fades with height, and by a kilometre or so up the wind runs almost exactly along the lines, while higher still it often blows from another direction altogether. That is why low clouds and high clouds often move in different directions.

The slant matters more than it looks. All round a low, the surface wind leaks inwards, so air piles up in the middle. It cannot go down, so it goes up, and rising air cools and forms cloud (Lesson 1). That is why lows bring cloud and rain. Around a high it is the other way: the wind spirals out clockwise, and air sinks from above to replace it, warming as it is squeezed and drying out its clouds, like Lesson 2’s lid. Highs bring clear skies.

blocks.caption: A low and a high seen from above (top) and from the side (bottom), in the northern half of the world.

blocks.text: The balance also tells you how hard it will blow. Since the push depends on how crowded the isobars are, and the wind speeds up until the turn matches the push, crowded isobars mean strong wind: twice the push needs twice the turn to balance it, and that takes roughly twice the wind. A forecaster with a fresh weather map can read the wind off it before going outside.[^map]

High above the ground, with no friction to slow it, the wind blows harder than at the surface, and it gets stronger with height for a reason of its own. Pressure at any height is the weight of the air above that height. Cold air is denser than warm air, so the same amount of air packs into a shallower layer over the cold Arctic than over the warm tropics. Climb ten kilometres over the Arctic and you have climbed past more of its squashed-down air than you would have over Hawaii, so less air is left above you: the pressure up there is much lower over the Arctic than at the same height over Hawaii. The push from high to low is therefore towards the pole, and it grows with height.

The turning Earth bends that poleward push into a wind blowing from west to east: the **westerlies**, which carry weather across the Pacific and over Washington from the west. They are strongest where cold and warm air meet most sharply, in a narrow ribbon about 9 to 12 kilometres up called the **jet stream**, where the wind often blows at 150 to 300 kilometres an hour, faster in winter.[^discovery]

Lows ride along under the jet stream like leaves on a river, steered from west to east along its waves. And the jet moves with the seasons. In winter, when the polar air is coldest and the contrast with the tropics is sharpest, the jet is strong and lies far to the south, aimed at Oregon and Washington, and storm after storm comes ashore. In summer, the contrast weakens, the jet slackens and retreats north towards Alaska, and the storms pass north of us.

blocks.caption: The jet stream across the North Pacific in winter and in summer, and the lows it carries east.

blocks.text: That is half of the reason why the Pacific Northwest has wet winters and dry summers. The other half is a great high that settles off the coast in summer, which is where the next lesson begins.
Use the push, the turn and friction to read the wind in the scenarios below.

blocks.caption: A sky, and what the map and the wind say. What is going on?

items.question: Air is moving north across Washington. Which way does the turning Earth bend it?
options: To its left, towards the west
To its right, towards the east
Not at all, since it moves due north
items.why: North of the equator the turning Earth bends moving air to its right, whichever way it is going, north included. South of the equator it bends it to the left.

instruments: Map: isobars twice as close as yesterday
items.question: The noon weather map shows the isobars over your town packed twice as close together as they were yesterday. What should you expect from the wind?
options: Stronger winds: crowded isobars mean a steep push, and the wind speeds up until the turn matches it
Calmer winds: crowded isobars mean the air is boxed in
The wind will blow straight across the isobars into the low
items.why: The push depends on how crowded the isobars are, and the wind speeds up until the Earth’s turn balances it. Twice the crowding means roughly twice the wind.

items.question: A ship’s officer who has sailed near the equator tells you that the winds there rarely circle round lows the way they do off Washington. Why not?
options: The air there is too warm to move
There is no difference in pressure anywhere near the equator
The ground at the equator does not turn under the moving air, so nothing bends the wind along the isobars
items.why: The drift from the turning Earth is strongest at the poles and vanishes at the equator. Without it, there is no balance to send the wind along the isobars.

items.question: The surface wind blows from the south, slanting across the isobars towards the low, but the cirrus overhead streams from the southwest, along them. Why the difference?
options: The cirrus is pushed by the sunlight
Friction with the ground slows the surface wind, so the Earth’s turn weakens and the push towards the low wins a little
The upper air feels no push from pressure
items.why: High up there is no friction, so the push and the turn balance and the wind runs along the isobars. Near the ground, friction slows the wind, the turn weakens, and the wind leaks across the lines into the low.

instruments: Barometer: high and steady for a week
items.question: A big high has sat over eastern Washington for a week of clear, still days. What is the air above it doing?
options: Sinking and spreading out, warming as it is squeezed, which keeps clouds away
Spiralling anticlockwise into the middle of the high
items.why: Around a high, the surface wind spirals out clockwise, and air sinks from above to replace it. Sinking air is squeezed and warms, so its clouds dry up.

learned: Air is pushed from high pressure towards low, straight across the isobars, hardest where they crowd together.

The Earth turns under moving air, so over hundreds of kilometres the air drifts to the right of its path north of the equator (to the left south of it). The turn is strongest at the poles and vanishes at the equator.

Aloft, the push and the turn balance when the wind runs along the isobars with the low on its left (the geostrophic wind): lows spin anticlockwise in the northern half of the world, and Buys Ballot’s rule follows.

Near the ground, friction slows the wind and it leaks across the isobars into a low (10° to 20° over sea, 25° to 40° over land); the air piles up and rises into cloud. Around a high, air sinks, warms and clears.
The westerlies grow with height and peak in the jet stream, 9 to 12 km up. It steers lows east, lies far south in winter (aimed at Oregon and Washington) and retreats north in summer.

pressure-push.title: Air slides downhill
pressure-push.text: Air is pushed from high pressure to low, straight across the isobars. Crowded isobars mean a steep push and a strong wind.

earth-turn.title: The ground turns underneath
earth-turn.text: Air moving freely over long distances drifts to the right of its path north of the equator, because the ground turns under it: a full circle a day at the pole, none at the equator. Too small to matter in a sink.

geostrophic.title: Round the low
geostrophic.text: Aloft, the push towards the low and the Earth’s turn balance when the wind runs along the isobars, low on its left. Near the ground, friction lets the wind leak in, and the air in a low rises into cloud; over a high it sinks and clears.

jet.title: The jet stream
jet.text: A ribbon of fast westerly wind 9 to 12 km up, where polar and tropical air meet. It steers lows east, sits far south in winter and retreats north in summer.

gradient.title: Pressure gradient
gradient.text: How fast the pressure changes with distance, and the push it puts on the air, the **pressure-gradient force**. Isobars 4 hPa apart and 100 km apart make a typical gradient; half the spacing, twice the push.

sinks.title: Sinks and toilets
sinks.text: The story that water drains clockwise in one hemisphere and anticlockwise in the other is a myth. The Earth’s turn is real but so slight over a few seconds that it only shows in a carefully built experiment: in 1962 Ascher Shapiro at MIT let a wide, still tank settle for a day before pulling the plug, and the water then drained anticlockwise every time.

geostrophic.title: Geostrophic wind
geostrophic.text: The wind that blows when the pressure push and the Earth’s turn exactly balance: along the isobars, low on its left (north of the equator), faster where they crowd. It describes the wind a kilometre or more up, above the drag of the ground, quite well.

map.title: The daily map in 1931
map.text: The Weather Bureau’s daily map was drawn by hand twice a day from barometer, wind and sky reports sent in by telegraph from some two hundred stations at the same moment, 8 a.m. and 8 p.m. Eastern Time. Isobars were sketched through the readings, and the wind arrows almost always ran along them.

discovery.title: Finding the jet stream
discovery.text: In the 1920s Wasaburo Oishi tracked hundreds of balloons over Tateno, Japan, and found winds of more than 200 km/h high above Mount Fuji, but he published in Esperanto and few read it. The German meteorologist Heinrich Seilkopf named the *Strahlströmung*, jet stream, in 1939, and in 1944 American bombers over Japan met headwinds so strong they barely moved over the ground.
